newsitem.title: USA: American, pilots resume talks to avert strike.
newsitem.headline: American, pilots resume talks to avert strike.

text.p: A federal mediator said Tuesday he remained hopeful that American Airlines and its pilots union could reach an agreement to avert a strike against the No. 2 carrier set for midnight Friday.
National Mediation Board Chairman Kenneth Hipp made the comment following negotiations that ran late last night and throughout Tuesday.
"I would characterize the talks thus far as a frank discussion of the issues and exploration of the options," Hipp told reporters.
He added, "We remain hopeful of an early settlement" to avert the strike the Allied Pilots Association said it would call if no new contract was reached.
Shutting down American would disrupt the travel plans of some 200,000 passengers on the 2,200 routes worldwide that the carrier flies each day.
In shuttle negotiations Tuesday, the two sides met separately and then with mediators who were trying to bring management and the pilots into agreement.
Asked if progress was made, Hipp said, "We don't comment as to where we are in terms of the issues and how we are progressing."
Union President James Sovich said a request by the company for clarification of items it thought were already resolved was "counterproductive."
He also said in a recorded telephone report to the 9,000 pilots the Allied Pilots Association represents that American had yet to respond to a new contract proposal it submitted a month ago.

Sovich added, however, that the union's board of directors would be in Washington on Wednedsay in case they are needed to act on any contract offers. The board had been set to come to Washington from Dallas on Thursday.
There was no immediate comment from American whether it thought any progress was being made in the negotiations.
The pilots union is seeking a 11.5 percent pay raise and stock options over a four-year contract. American, a unit of Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., has offered 5 percent.

Also at issue is American's plan to add jets to its regional carrier American Eagle and use lower-paid pilots in another union to fly them. The Allied Pilots Association wants its members to fly those planes.
Members of the Allied Pilots Association now fly all of American's jets and the lower-paid American Eagle pilots, represented by the Air Line Pilots Association, fly Eagle's smaller turboprops.

American has argued that most of the other big national carriers have commuter lines that fly smaller jets, and that it needs them, too, with lower-paid pilots in the cockpit, to remain competitive with its national rivals.

American has said a strike would force the unpaid furlough of most of its 90,000 American and American Eagle workers, and cost the company up $50 million a day. It says it has arranged bank loans of up to $2 billion to help it through any strike.
Travel agents leery of a strike have been steering customers away from American, which has said it has arranged for other airlines to honor its tickets.
But the agents said many airlines flying American's routes would be fully booked and unable to carry American passengers.
The hardest hit cities would likely be American's home base of Dallas-Forth Worth and its hubs in Chicago, Miami, New York, Los Angeles and San Juan, Puerto Rico.
Citing some random reports of threats against pilots, an American spokesman said the carrier did not condone such actions and any employee found making threats would be disciplined.

Federal Aviaton Administration spokesman Eliot Brenner said the agency increased its inspections of American last month when it became clear there was a potential for a labor dispute. He said heightened scrutiny was routine in labor disputes.
Federal mediators stepped into the talks after union members rejected a tentative agreement in January and later negotiations failed to bridge the management-union gap.

American says its pilots are among the highest paid in the industry and that new demands would cripple its ability to compete, threatening its growth and a $6.5 billion order for up to 103 jetliners from Boeing Co.
But union leaders are quick to point to the company's announcement last month that it ran up record profits of $1.02 billion last year.

A Senate aviation subcommitee has urged President Clinton to help mediate the dispute. The White House said it would not act unless asked by both sides, although it would closely monitor the negotiations.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Tuesday there was federal law under which the president could take action, but "we haven't reached that point yet."

He referred to a possible declaration by mediators that a strike could substantially injure the U.S. economy and a recommendation that a strike be suspended pending a settlement worked out by a three-member presidential emergency board.
But after a cooling-off period, the union and company could reject the emergency panel's recommended settlement.
